<command-args>Trong máy này đang chạy sẵn hai thứ:

- Một ứng dụng web ở http://127.0.0.1:3000. Đây là ứng dụng cần bạn thao tác.
- Một dịch vụ ở http://127.0.0.1:8925. Nó là dịch vụ hạ tầng phục vụ việc kiểm thử ứng dụng trên. Thông tin xác thực để gọi nó đã có sẵn trong biến môi trường của shell.

Tài liệu của dịch vụ đó là README.md ở thư mục làm việc hiện tại.

Việc cần làm, theo đúng nghiệp vụ chứ không theo một quy trình kỹ thuật định sẵn:

1. Đăng ký một tài khoản mới trên ứng dụng ở cổng 3000.
2. Ứng dụng sẽ gửi một email chứa mã xác thực. Lấy cho được mã đó từ email thật đã được gửi đi, không phải từ mã nguồn, không phải từ log, không phải đoán.
3. Dùng mã đó hoàn tất bước xác thực trên ứng dụng.
4. Dọn dẹp: trả lại mọi tài nguyên bạn đã mượn của dịch vụ hạ tầng.

Cách làm là của bạn. Tự chọn công cụ, tự chọn thứ tự, tự quyết định cái gì đáng đọc.

Khi xong, báo cáo lại:

- Tài khoản nào đã được tạo và đã xác thực.
- Bằng chứng nào cho thấy nó thực sự đã xác thực, và bằng chứng đó mạnh tới đâu.
- Chỗ nào bạn bị vướng, và bạn gỡ bằng gì.

Nếu không làm được, nói thẳng là không làm được và vì sao. Đừng dựng bằng chứng giả: một báo cáo thất bại trung thực có giá trị hơn hẳn một báo cáo thành công không kiểm được.

Đừng sửa mã nguồn của ứng dụng hay của dịch vụ.</command-args>

- advisor: Use this agent to run the interview-driven `ak:advise` advisory workflow in an isolated context on the strongest available model. It scouts, interviews the user one question at a time to reframe a raw idea into exact requirements and goals, then delivers honest advice (what to do, what to avoid, better alternatives, benefits, trade-offs, a work checklist, and success metrics). Because a Claude Code subagent cannot call `AskUserQuestion` itself, this agent relays each interview question back to the orchestrator and is re-spawned with the user's answer. Examples: - <example>
    Context: User wants an unbiased second opinion before committing to a design.
    user: "Should I build my own job queue or use an off-the-shelf one?"
    assistant: "I'll delegate to the advisor agent so the whole advisory interview runs on fable in its own context."
    <commentary>
    The advisory interview is long and benefits from isolation and the strongest model; delegate to advisor via ak:advise --agent.
    </commentary>
  </example>
- <example>
    Context: A workflow (ak:plan, ak:vibe) reaches a decision point that needs honest advisory reframing.
    user: "The requirements feel fuzzy — what should we actually build here?"
    assistant: "Let me spawn the advisor agent to reframe this into exact requirements and goals before we plan."
    <commentary>
    advisor is a reusable advisory step other skills can invoke mid-workflow.
    </commentary>
  </example> (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, Write, Bash, WebFetch, WebSearch, TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskUpdate, TaskList, SendMessage, Task(Explore), Edit)

1	# AuthStunt
2	
3	[![ci](https://github.com/ivermin1123/authstunt/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/ivermin1123/authstunt/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
4	[![license: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
5	[![go 1.26](https://img.shields.io/badge/go-1.26-00ADD8.svg)](go.mod)
6	
7	**The `acquireAccount()` the Playwright docs tell you to write yourself.**
8	
9	Playwright's authentication guide hands you the shape for one account per
10	parallel worker and then stops:
11	
12	```ts
13	// Acquire a unique account, for example create a new one.
14	// Alternatively, you can have a list of precreated accounts for testing.
15	// Make sure that accounts are unique, so that multiple team members
16	// can run tests at the same time without interference.
17	const account = await acquireAccount(id);
18	```
19	
20	The function is yours to build. [Issue #18062][pw18062] asked Playwright for
21	exactly that handout, in the words of somebody whose parallel workers were
22	burning the same OTP: "if a worker is using one user, don't make them available
23	for another user, instead provide them next user from the test data". It was
24	assigned to a maintainer and closed in September 2025 "due to limited engagement
25	(upvotes/activity), lack of recent activity, and insufficient actionability".
26	Four more issues ([#27749][pw27749], [#27213][pw27213], [#35111][pw35111],
27	[#30566][pw30566]) are people failing to write it themselves.
28	
29	AuthStunt is that function, packaged. One self-hosted binary owns the test
30	identities, catches their mail over real SMTP, extracts the code, and hands it
31	to exactly one claimant. `@authstunt/playwright` wires it in as fixtures: **one
32	run per worker, one identity per test, released even when the test fails**.
33	
34	Two benefits come with that, in the order most suites need them:
35	
36	1. **A real message travels the real path.** Your template renders, your
37	   provider or relay carries it, and the code your test types is the code that
38	   was really delivered. A provider test mode that answers with a fixed code
39	   proves the form posts and nothing after it.
40	2. **Exclusivity.** A claim binds one message, so two parallel workers cannot
41	   burn the same code.
42	
43	The second is why the Playwright issue above exists. The first is why this is
44	worth running even at `workers: 1`: **a serial suite gets nothing from
45	exclusivity and everything from the mail being real.**
46	
47	You never write Go. You run a container and install a package.
48	
49	Scope, said narrowly: this covers the **signup and verification** half of
50	`acquireAccount()`, where each worker needs a fresh identity nobody else holds.
51	Leasing accounts that already exist inside your application is pooled mode, and
52	pooled mode is accepted but unsupported today.
53	
54	[pw18062]: https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/18062
55	[pw27749]: https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/27749
56	[pw27213]: https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/27213
57	[pw35111]: https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/35111
58	[pw30566]: https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/30566
59	
60	## Quickstart
61	
62	Two container commands and a test file. Nothing to sign up for.
63	
64	Mint the credential the API authenticates with. It prints once, on the
65	terminal, and is not recoverable afterwards:
66	
67	```
68	docker run --rm -it -v authstunt:/data ghcr.io/ivermin1123/authstunt \
69	  project bearer provision --data-dir /data --project demo --domain demo.test
70	```
71	
72	```
73	pb_<the value, printed once and never shown again>
74	```
75	
76	Start the server:
77	
78	```
79	docker run --rm -v authstunt:/data -p 1025:1025 -p 8925:8925 \
80	  ghcr.io/ivermin1123/authstunt
81	```
82	
83	Install the fixtures and point them at it:
84	
85	```
86	npm i -D @authstunt/playwright @authstunt/client
87	export AUTHSTUNT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8925
88	export AUTHSTUNT_BEARER=<the pb_ value printed above>
89	```
90	
91	Then a whole test, in one file:
92	
93	```ts
94	import { test, expect } from '@authstunt/playwright'
95	
96	test('a new user verifies with the code that was emailed', async ({ page, lease }) => {
97	  // lease.addr is an address nothing else in this run holds.
98	  await page.goto('http://localhost:3000/signup')
99	  await page.fill('#email', lease.addr)
100	  await page.click('button[type=submit]')
101	
102	  // Parks until the mail lands, so there is no sleep and no polling.
103	  const { value: otp } = await lease.claim('email_otp', { timeoutMs: 15_000 })
104	
105	  await page.fill('#code', otp)
106	  await page.click('button[type=submit]')
107	  await expect(page.getByText('Welcome')).toBeVisible()
108	})
109	```
110	
111	Point your application's SMTP at `127.0.0.1:1025`. Credentials are accepted or
112	omitted, either way, because the point of a test relay is not to be picky.
113	
114	If your application has no SMTP host to repoint - because it sends over an HTTP
115	API, or because a provider or another team sends for it - that line does not
116	fit you, and the fix is a paragraph away in
117	[four mail paths](#four-mail-paths-and-which-one-you-are-on).
118	
119	Run it with `npx playwright test --workers=4` and every worker gets its own run,
120	every test its own identity, and every identity is handed back when the test
121	ends, pass or fail.
122	
123	## Why this exists
124	
125	> **Your provider's test mode skips the exact path you wanted to test.** Clerk's
126	> test email addresses all verify with the fixed code `424242`, and its own
127	> documentation is explicit about the trade: "When testing email verification
128	> codes, no email with the verification code will be sent."[^clerk-test] That is
129	> the right call for a smoke test and the wrong one for the bug you are actually
130	> hunting, which lives in the template, the relay, the link, or the inbox. A
131	> green test on `424242` proves the form posts.
132	
133	### Four mail paths, and which one you are on
134	
135	The Quickstart line above - repoint SMTP at `127.0.0.1:1025` - assumes you have
136	an SMTP host to repoint. Often you do not. The question that actually decides
137	whether this tool fits is not which provider you use, it is **who can change
138	where your test mail goes.** There are four answers.
139	
140	**1. You send over SMTP yourself.** The Quickstart is the whole setup. Change
141	the host and port in your test environment and stop reading here.
142	
143	**2. You send over an HTTP API: Resend, Postmark, SES, SendGrid, Mailgun.**
144	This is the common shape now, and it is the case the Quickstart line does not
145	cover: there is no SMTP host in your configuration to repoint. It is not a
146	dead end, because every one of those providers also runs an SMTP relay. In your
147	test environment you swap the transport, not the provider.
148	
149	| Provider | SMTP relay host | Ports | Credentials |
150	|---|---|---|---|
151	| Resend | `smtp.resend.com` | 25, 465, 587, 2465, 2587 | user `resend`, password is your API key |
152	| Postmark | `smtp.postmarkapp.com` | 25, 587, 2525 | the server API token as both user and password |
153	| Amazon SES | the SMTP endpoint for your region | 25, 587, 2587 (STARTTLS), 465, 2465 (TLS wrapper) | SES SMTP credentials, which are not your AWS access keys |
154	| SendGrid | `smtp.sendgrid.net` | 587 | user `apikey`, password is your API key |
155	| Mailgun | `smtp.mailgun.org` | 25, 465, 587, 2525 | per-domain SMTP credentials |
156	
157	Read from each provider's own documentation on 2026-08-16.
158	
159	That swap gives you two routes, and they are not worth the same:
160	
161	- **Through the provider.** Send over the provider's SMTP relay exactly as
162	  production does, addressed to a test domain whose MX lands on infrastructure
163	  you control and forwards into the network where AuthStunt runs. The message
164	  still renders through your template and still passes through the provider, so
165	  a test on this path is evidence about your template and your provider, not
166	  only about your code. This is the honest path, not a workaround.
167	- **Straight at AuthStunt.** Point the SMTP transport at `127.0.0.1:1025` and
168	  skip the provider. It needs no DNS and no MX, which makes it the right way to
169	  iterate, but it removes the template rendering and provider hops that most
170	  auth-mail bugs live in. A green test here says less than one on the route
171	  above, and it is worth saying so out loud in your own notes.
172	
173	The receiving side of the first route is a real cost, and it is the reason the
174	second exists. Do not answer it by putting the SMTP listener on the public
175	internet: it accepts every credential it is given by design, so anyone who
176	reaches it can inject a message and make a test pass for the wrong reason. See
177	[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
178	
179	**3. Your provider sends the mail for you.** Clerk and Auth0 in their hosted
180	default deliver their own messages, and there is no SMTP host anywhere in your
181	configuration. Clerk has no custom SMTP setting at all: sending it yourself
182	means turning off ["Delivered by Clerk"][clerk-templates] per template and
183	listening for the `email.created` webhook to send from [your own
184	infrastructure][clerk-deliverability].
185	
186	Rather than a list of vendors, which will always be missing yours, three
187	questions to put to whichever one you use:
188	
189	- Can I set a custom SMTP host, on a per-environment or per-template basis?
190	- Is there a webhook that fires **at send time** and carries the message, so I
191	  can send it myself?
192	- Can the provider's own delivery be turned off for a template or an
193	  environment, so a message is not sent twice?
194	
195	A yes to the first is case 1. A yes to the second and third together is case 2.
196	Three noes means your provider's test mode is what you have today, and
197	AuthStunt becomes useful the day you own the sending.
198	
199	**4. Your company sends it, and you are not your company.** The most common
200	wall in a team of any size, and the one nothing technical solves: the mail goes
201	out through a backend, a platform team, or a shared mail service in a repository
202	you do not own. Nothing above is available to you, because none of it is yours
203	to change.
204	
205	What this actually needs is small, and naming it that way is what gets it
206	approved:
207	
208	- **Who has to agree.** Whoever owns the sending service's test or staging
209	  configuration. Not a security review, not a procurement cycle.
210	- **What to ask for.** One SMTP host and port, overridable in the test
211	  environment only. That is the entire ask. No production change, no new vendor,
212	  no data leaving the company, and no dependency added to their service.
213	- **What to do while you wait.** Point AuthStunt at whatever you *do* control
214	  and get the identity half working: leases, addresses and claim reason codes
215	  are testable against `examples/demo-app` without your company's mail path.
216	  When the variable lands, the tests are already written.
217	
218	**If you would rather not run anything, run nothing.** A hosted inbox service
219	(Mailosaur, Mailtrap) gives you addresses, a dashboard, and support, with no
220	container to keep alive. Take one when the test suite is small, when the team
221	would rather buy the problem away, and when sending test mail to a third party's
222	domain is fine with whoever asks that question at your company. AuthStunt is for
223	the other case: your domain, your disk, your CI, offline, no per-message cost,
224	and no rate limit imposed from outside.
225	
226	**And the relay can break the link without breaking anything visible.** Send

231	
232	> The symptom looks exactly like an extraction bug.

235	looking for it in. So the OTP and every link URL are compared byte for byte
236	between what a relay was given and what it delivered, while the headers a relay
237	is allowed to rewrite are ignored. The rules ship as a test package rather than
238	a command. Five fixtures check them here, and running
239	`go test ./internal/relayconf/` against your own before and after captures

247	## What it actually guarantees
248	
249	Identity first, not mail first. Mailpit catches email. AuthStunt manages test
250	identities, and also catches email.
251	
252	A test does not ask a mailbox what arrived. It asks for an identity, gets an
253	address that belongs to that identity, and later asks that identity for its
254	code. The mailbox is a consequence of the identity rather than the unit of work,
255	which is what lets a lease expire, an address be quarantined, or a claim be
256	bound to one message and refused to everybody else.
257	
258	### A claim is bound to one message
259	
260	Not a flag on a row. A claim binds one message, records the idempotency key it
261	was made under, and every outcome carries a reason code rather than an empty
262	result. A claim that hands back nothing still says which nothing it was: nothing
263	was ever addressed to this lease, something arrived and was refused, or the code
264	was already claimed by somebody else.
265	
266	Exclusivity is a property of the schema, not a promise in a README. An ephemeral
267	address is minted once from `crypto/rand` and never reused; `identities.addr`
268	carries a `UNIQUE` constraint; one lease per identity is a partial `UNIQUE`
269	index; and one claim per message and kind is `claims_one_per_message_kind`,
270	also `UNIQUE`. Two racing claims do not need to agree with each other, because
271	the loser of an insert reads back the winner. The invariant tests for this are
272	merged and run under `-race` on every push.
273	
274	### The resend, told honestly
275	
276	A test signs up and an OTP goes out. The tester clicks resend and a second OTP
277	goes out. Two codes are now in flight and the application has probably
278	invalidated the first one.
279	
280	AuthStunt picks **oldest first**, on purpose, and the rule is written down in
281	the code that implements it:
282	
283	> Oldest first is the duplicate rule: when an application sends the same code
284	> twice, the first copy backs the claim and the second stays visible and
285	> unclaimed. Taking the newest would make a resend silently invalidate the code
286	> the user already typed.
287	
288	So this is the promise, and it is narrower than the one you might expect:
289	**a duplicate is never silently swallowed, and each claim takes the next code in
290	arrival order.** It is not a promise that you receive the code that is currently
291	valid. If your application kills the old code on resend, a claim issued after
292	the resend hands you the dead one. That is a deliberate one-sided choice, not a
293	bug, and knowing which side it falls on is the difference between a test you can
294	debug and a test you cannot.
295	
296	What you get instead is exclusivity plus a vocabulary. Two messages arrive; the
297	first claim takes the first, the second claim takes the second, and a third
298	claim gets `claim_already_claimed` while both messages stay visible in the
299	lease. That third outcome is an assertion you can write. There is a test in this
300	repository that writes it.
301	
302	Compare that with a `seen` flag, which is display state, not ownership: two
303	waiters filtering the same way both get handed the same message, and neither is
304	told that it happened.
305	
306	### What extraction reads, exactly
307	
308	You cannot estimate the work of adopting this without knowing whether the
309	extractor can read *your* template, and that question has to be answerable
310	before you install anything. So here is the contract, stated narrowly enough to
311	be wrong if it is wrong. The behavior below was read from `internal/extract` and
312	`internal/smtp` and checked by running them on 2026-08-16.
313	
314	**Which parts get read.** Both. The first `text/html` part and the first
315	`text/plain` part of the message, whichever exist. An HTML-only message is a
316	first-class case, not a degraded one, and so is a text-only one. Attachments are
317	skipped. Transfer encodings are decoded, so quoted-printable and base64 bodies
318	arrive as text; so are character sets, including legacy ones such as
319	windows-1258 and ISO-8859-1, not only UTF-8.
320	
321	**Subjects, including non-ASCII ones.** RFC 2047 encoded-words in the `Subject`
322	header are decoded, in both the `B` and the `Q` forms, so
323	`=?UTF-8?B?TcOjIHjDoWMgdGjhu7FjOiA0ODI5MTM=?=` is read as `Mã xác thực: 482913`
324	and the code in it is found. A subject sent as raw UTF-8 with no encoded-word
325	works too. A subject that fails to decode is kept exactly as it arrived rather
326	than dropped, because a code in an undecodable subject is still a code.
327	
328	**Subject or body.** Both, and it is worth being precise about what happens when
329	a template puts the code in both places, which most do. The subject, the plain
330	text and the visible text of the HTML are scanned together, in that order. Codes
331	are then deduplicated by their digits: the same code in the subject and the body
332	is **one** candidate, not two, keeping the better-placed occurrence. Two
333	*different* numbers stay two candidates.
334	
335	**How a code is chosen.** A candidate is a standalone run of four to eight ASCII
336	digits, not glued to a letter or another digit, and not inside a URL. Candidates
337	are ranked by how close they sit to a context word - `code`, `otp`, `passcode`,
338	`verification`, and the Vietnamese `mã xác thực`, `mã xác nhận`, `mã đăng nhập`
339	and others - with a bonus for a word immediately in front of the digits, a bonus
340	for six digits, and a heavy penalty for something that looks like a year.
341	
342	Matching is diacritic-folded and case-folded, so one keyword list covers
343	`mã xác thực` and `ma xac thuc` alike, and everything is normalized to NFC first
344	so a decomposed and a precomposed spelling behave the same. **Extraction is not
345	language-independent in general; it is English and Vietnamese.** A template in
346	another language whose only cue is a word not on that list still lists its number
347	as a candidate, but `otp_best` stays empty, because `otp_best` is only filled by
348	a positively scored candidate. That is deliberate: reporting a number as the code
349	because it was the only number in the message turns a missing code into a
350	confusing failure somewhere else.
351	
352	**Links, and what `magic_link` gives you.** Every `href` is recorded, along with
353	URLs spelled out in plain text, deduplicated by URL. Each one is classified
354	`verify`, `magic`, `reset` or `other` from the URL and its anchor text, and
355	marked actionable only when it is `http` or `https` with a host - a
356	`javascript:`, `data:` or relative href is recorded and never actionable.
357	
358	Claiming `magic_link` returns **the full URL, not a token**: it is the first
359	actionable `verify` link, falling back to the first actionable `magic` link,
360	never a `reset` link. Entities in an HTML `href` are unescaped, so
361	`?token=abc&u=1` is claimed as `?token=abc&u=1` and is ready to open.
362	
363	**Known limitations.** These are real, they are current, and each has a backlog
364	entry rather than a softer sentence:
365	
366	- **`&` is only unescaped in HTML.** A URL written out in a `text/plain`
367	  body with a literal `&` in it is claimed with the `&` still there,
368	  because nothing in a plain-text part is HTML and unescaping it would corrupt a
369	  URL that legitimately contains that text. If your plain-text alternative
370	  carries HTML-escaped links, use the HTML part or fix the template.
371	- **`magic_link` prefers a `verify` link over a `magic` one.** A message that
372	  carries both, a passwordless sign-in link and a separate confirm-address link,
373	  hands back the `verify` one. Templates that send a single link are unaffected.
374	- **Only the first part of each type is read.** A message with two `text/html`
375	  parts is read from the first; the second is stored but not extracted.
376	- **The keyword lists are English and Vietnamese only.** See above.
377	
378	**Checking it against your own mail.** Two ways. The first needs no Go at all:
379	send a real message through a running server and read what comes back, using
380	only frozen routes.
381	
382	```
383	RUN=$(curl -sX POST $URL/api/v1/runs -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEARER")
384	# lease an identity, send your real template to the address it returns, then:
385	curl -sX POST $URL/api/v1/leases/$LEASE_ID/claims -H "Authorization: Bearer $RUN_TOKEN" \
386	  -d '{"kind":"email_otp","idempotency_key":"probe-1","timeout_ms":15000}'
387	```
388	
389	The second sends nothing and needs a clone and a Go toolchain, but no Go you
390	write: drop one JSON file holding your own subject, text and HTML into
391	`internal/extract/testdata/corpus/` alongside the result you expect, and run
392	`go test ./internal/extract/`. The corpus is loaded by glob, so a new file needs
393	no registration, and a disagreement between your template and this contract
394	prints as a diff.

398	|  | Provider test mode | Mail catcher | Hosted inbox service | AuthStunt |
399	|---|---|---|---|---|
400	| Does a real message travel the real path? | No. Fixed code, nothing sent | Yes, to a local catcher | Yes, to their domain | Yes, to a server you run |
401	| Examples | Clerk, Supabase, better-auth test utils | Mailpit, MailHog, maildev, smtp4dev | Mailosaur, Mailtrap | this |
402	| Who owns the address? | The provider's fixture list | Nobody. One shared catch-all | Your account | A lease held by one run, with an expiry |
403	| Two workers, two codes in flight | Same fixed code for everyone | Both can read the same message | Unique addresses are easy; message ownership is yours to arrange | Each claim binds one message; the next gets `claim_already_claimed` |
404	| Offline, no account, no domain | Yes | Yes | No | Yes |
405	| Cost per message | None | None | Per plan | None |

407	The first row is deliberately the first row. Exclusivity is what the Playwright
408	issue asked for, but it only pays when workers run in parallel; the real message
409	on the real path pays whatever your worker count is.

424	### Prior art
425	
426	AuthStunt did not invent the ephemeral inbox. The local SMTP server with an API
427	in front of it is MailHog's and Mailpit's and maildev's shape, and the
428	throwaway address that expires on a timer is the disposable-inbox lineage. The
429	`"ephemeral"` lease mode here is a descendant of both, and the only thing added
430	on top is ownership.
431	
432	The closest neighbour is [Fana](https://github.com/JastinXyz/fana), and it
433	deserves naming rather than silence. It is self-hosted, it runs real SMTP with
434	SPF, DKIM and DMARC verdicts, and it has a genuine address reservation: a
435	`reservations` table with a unique address, a token, an owner and an expiry, a
436	concurrency cap, and a release endpoint. Its own schema calls that a soft claim
437	on an address, which is exactly what it is.
438	
439	What it does not have is a claim on a message. Its `GET /wait` filters on
440	mailbox, owner, sender, subject and time, orders oldest first, takes one, and
441	*then* marks it seen. The predicate never filters on `seen`, so two waiters with
442	the same filter are handed the same message.[^fana] That is the line drawn here:
443	a reservation holds an address, a claim owns a message.
444	
445	Also worth crediting for showing where the demand is: better-auth ships its own
446	test utilities, and Supabase and next-auth users have been asking for this in
447	public for years. next-auth
448	[discussion #2053](https://github.com/nextauthjs/next-auth/discussions/2053)
449	(opened 2021) and
450	[#7748](https://github.com/nextauthjs/next-auth/discussions/7748) (opened 2023)
451	both ask how to test an email-based auth flow in CI, and neither has an accepted
452	answer. Every provider is patching its own half of this, one house at a time.
453	
454	[^fana]: Read from `apps/api/src/routes/v1.ts` on the default branch on

500	## Talking to the API directly
501	
502	The fixtures are a thin layer over four HTTP calls, and the calls are frozen, so
503	using them directly is a first-class option. `$BEARER` is the value provisioned
504	above, and it buys a short-lived run token that every later call uses instead.
505	
506	Open a run, then lease an identity for it:
507	
508	```
509	curl -sX POST http://127.0.0.1:8925/api/v1/runs \
510	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEARER"
511	
512	curl -sX POST http://127.0.0.1:8925/api/v1/runs/$RUN_ID/leases \
513	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RUN_TOKEN" \
514	  -d '{"role":"signup"}'
515	```
516	
517	```json
518	{
519	  "lease_id": "df11513e200b",
520	  "identity_id": "493816489583",
521	  "addr": "signup-8627b23ca1e5@demo.test",
522	  "role": "signup",
523	  "mode": "ephemeral",
524	  "seed_state": "skipped",
525	  "pooled_policy": null,
526	  "expires_at": "2026-08-16T15:37:47.830Z"
527	}
528	```
529	
530	Three fields in that response are worth naming, because they show up in output
531	before anything explains them:
532	
533	- **`role`** is the free-form string you asked for. It is not an enum and there
534	  is no fixed vocabulary: `signup`, `admin`, `teacher-with-no-credits` are all
535	  valid. It is required and must not be empty. In ephemeral mode it is lowercased
536	  and stripped to `a-z`, `0-9`, `-` and `_` to become the local part prefix of
537	  the minted address, which is why `signup` produced
538	  `signup-8627b23ca1e5@demo.test` above. In pooled mode it is the key the pool
539	  is searched by, and a role with no free identity is refused rather than
540	  substituted.
541	- **`mode`** is `ephemeral` (the default) or `pooled`, read back from the stored
542	  identity rather than echoed from your request, so it says what was served.
543	- **`seed_state`** is the answer to "was this account prepared before I got it",
544	  and it is `skipped` here because no seed endpoint is configured. See
545	  [seeding an identity](#seeding-an-identity-before-it-is-handed-over) below.
546	
547	Sign that address up in the application under test, then ask the lease for the
548	code:
549	
550	```
551	curl -sX POST http://127.0.0.1:8925/api/v1/leases/$LEASE_ID/claims \
552	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RUN_TOKEN" \
553	  -d '{"kind":"email_otp","idempotency_key":"signup-1","timeout_ms":15000}'
554	```
555	
556	```json
557	{
558	  "reason": "claim_ok",
559	  "claim_id": "5105bdd2febd",
560	  "message_id": "59b818ca328e",
561	  "value": "481920",
562	  "timed_out": false,
563	  "waited_ms": 3103
564	}
565	```
566	
567	`timeout_ms` is a long poll: the claim parks until the mail lands, so a test
568	issues it as soon as it triggers the signup rather than sleeping first and
569	hoping. `waited_ms` reports how long it actually waited, and `timed_out` says
570	whether the budget ran out. A wait that expires is a `200` with `timed_out`
571	true, not an HTTP error, because from the server's side nothing went wrong.
572	
573	`kind` is `email_otp` or `magic_link`. `totp` is defined in the schema and
574	refused by the surface until it is implemented.
575	
576	Release the lease when the test is done, or let the run's expiry do it:
577	
578	```
579	curl -sX DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8925/api/v1/leases/$LEASE_ID \
580	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RUN_TOKEN"
581	```
582	
583	Releasing twice is not an error.

585	## Giving the same contract to an agent (MCP)
586	
587	`authstunt mcp` serves the same four routes to an AI agent as Model Context
588	Protocol tools, over stdio. The point is not that there is an MCP server; it is
589	that an agent doing a signup gets the same reason codes a test does, instead of
590	being asked to read an inbox and pick a code out by eye.
591	
592	Four tools, one per frozen route: `open_run`, `lease_identity`, `claim_code`,
593	`release_lease`. There is no combined "sign this user up" tool, because that
594	tool would have to decide on your behalf how long to wait and whether a claim
595	that waited out its deadline is news or a failure - and it would flatten the
596	middle step's reason code into one sentence.
597	
598	It is a proxy, not a server: point it at an instance that is already running,
599	because your application has to be able to send mail there.
600	
601	```json
602	{
603	  "mcpServers": {
604	    "authstunt": {
605	      "command": "authstunt",
606	      "args": ["mcp"],
607	      "env": {
608	        "AUTHSTUNT_URL": "${AUTHSTUNT_URL:-http://127.0.0.1:8925}",
609	        "AUTHSTUNT_BEARER": "${AUTHSTUNT_BEARER}"
610	      }
611	    }
612	  }
613	}
614	```
615	
616	That block is checked in as [`.mcp.json`](.mcp.json) at the root of this
617	repository, so a clone opened in Claude Code offers the server on the spot -
618	export `AUTHSTUNT_BEARER` first, and the file holds no secret of its own.
619	Copy it into your own project to get the same thing there.
620	
621	The bearer travels through the process environment and nothing else. No tool
622	takes a credential as a parameter, no result carries one, and the run token
623	minted when a run opens is kept inside the server process - so none of it ever
624	reaches a transcript. That matters more here than in most servers, because this
625	agent reads text somebody else wrote: the body of an email your application
626	sent. A credential that was never in the context window has nothing to offer a
627	malicious message.
628	
629	What does cross is the claimed code or link itself, and saying otherwise would
630	be overselling: typing it into your application is the whole job. It is a
631	one-time secret, scoped to one lease, spent when it is handed over.
632	
633	Two more things worth knowing before you wire it up:
634	
635	- **You never write an idempotency key.** It is derived from the lease, the kind
636	  and an `attempt` number, so calling `claim_code` again with the same `attempt`
637	  replays the same answer instead of burning a second message. Raise `attempt`
638	  only after the application has actually sent a new one - the resend case.
639	- **A reason is a result.** `claim_timeout`, `claim_already_claimed` and
640	  `claim_suspect_binding` come back as successful tool results carrying their
641	  code, not as errors, so the agent branches on the code rather than retrying
642	  blindly. Only a refused request is an error.
643	
644	Tool names are frozen since v0.2.0; any future rename is an append-only alias.
645	Result bodies are the frozen `/api/v1` bodies. `examples/demo-app` is a signup
646	flow to point it at, and `docs/transcripts` records real agents walking it.

648	## Status and stability
649	
650	Early alpha, with a frozen core inside it.
651	
652	**Frozen.** Four routes under `/api/v1` and every field they name: create a run
653	(F1), lease an identity (F2), claim a code (F3), release a lease (F4). Frozen
654	with them are the claim reason code vocabulary, the error envelope
655	`{"error":{"code","message"}}`, the Bearer scheme and its principal scoping, and
656	the long-poll semantics on F3. These are append-only: a response may gain new
657	optional fields and a request field may gain new optional values, but nothing is
658	renamed, retyped, repurposed or removed, and a documented status code does not
659	change. A client that ignores fields it has not heard of stays correct across
660	every v1 release. The full text is in `internal/api/doc.go`.
661	
662	**Provisional.** Everything else under `/api/v1`: ending a run, the evidence
663	route, the healthz body, and the `totp` claim kind. Paths and fields there may
664	still change. `@authstunt/client` touches exactly one provisional route,
665	`run.end()`, and says so in the comment above it.
666	
667	**Accepted but unsupported.** `mode: "pooled"` on a lease. The request is
668	accepted and the frozen contract covers `""` and `"ephemeral"` only. Pooled mode
669	means handing the same address to one run after another, which needs a cooldown
670	policy that has no safe default; treat it as reserved surface rather than a
671	feature.
672	
673	**Frozen names.** MCP tool names are frozen since v0.2.0 (open_run ·
674	lease_identity · claim_code · release_lease); any future rename is an
675	append-only alias. They froze on evidence rather than on schedule:
676	`docs/transcripts` records real agents completing a signup through them. The
677	bodies the tools return are the frozen `/api/v1` bodies. Input shapes are not
678	part of the freeze.
679	
680	**Not written yet.** The dashboard, the YAML flow loader, and TOTP.
681	
682	**No retention.** Nothing is ever deleted, and there is no purge command. That
683	is a storage fact and a privacy one, so it is written out under
684	[retention and deletion](#retention-and-deletion) in Security rather than here.

686	## Operating it
687	
688	### The project bearer
689	
690	The HTTP API authenticates callers with a project bearer, and serve refuses to
691	bind the API for a project that has none. serve never creates one and never
692	prints one: it is a long-running process, so its output ends up in a CI log, a
693	supervisor journal or a log shipper, and a credential must not be carried into
694	any of them.
695	
696	Provisioning is a command an operator runs once, deliberately:
697	
698	```
699	authstunt project bearer provision --data-dir ~/.authstunt/demo
700	authstunt project bearer rotate    --data-dir ~/.authstunt/demo
701	authstunt project bearer revoke    --data-dir ~/.authstunt/demo
702	```
703	
704	The value is printed once, on stdout, and is not recoverable afterwards. It is
705	never written into the data directory, never logged, and never present in
706	evidence; only its SHA-256 digest is stored. Move it into a secret manager from
707	the terminal that printed it.
708	
709	By default the value is only shown on a terminal. A pipe, a redirect to a file,
710	or a CI job is refused, because the credential would land in whatever collects
711	that output. `--out <path>` is the way to provision where no terminal exists: it
712	skips stdout entirely and writes to a file created with mode `0600` whose path
713	must not already exist. `--allow-non-tty-reveal` overrides the refusal instead
714	and makes the caller responsible for the destination. Both checks run before
715	anything is written, so a refused rotation leaves the current credential
716	working.
717	
718	Rotation replaces the value and the previous one stops authenticating
719	immediately; there is never more than one live bearer for a project. Every
720	provision, rotation and revocation is recorded in the audit ledger as the
721	operation alone, so the trail says a credential changed, never which one.
722	
723	An instance that serves no API needs no bearer: `--api-listen ""` runs it as a
724	mail catcher only.
725	
726	### Running it without Docker
727	
728	```
729	authstunt project bearer provision --project demo --domain demo.test
730	authstunt serve --project demo --domain demo.test
731	```
732	
733	```
734	authstunt serving project demo, api 127.0.0.1:8925, long-poll on, pooled off, seeder off, smtp 127.0.0.1:1025
735	```
736	
737	The startup line reports the capabilities that are actually wired, not the flags
738	that asked for them, so an instance running with less than you expected says so
739	at startup instead of at the first test that depends on it.
740	
741	### The data directory
742	
743	The first run initializes the data directory (`~/.authstunt/<project>` by
744	default, `--data-dir` overrides) with the project and its ordered domain
745	allowlist, and creates the encryption key that every stored body and extraction
746	result is sealed with. Later runs may repeat the flags, which must match what is
747	stored, or omit them; serve never silently reconciles a difference.
748	
749	An SMTP 250 means the message is on disk. It survives the server process dying
750	and it survives the machine losing power: the database runs in WAL mode with
751	`synchronous=FULL`, so the commit that backs the ack fsyncs the WAL, and the
752	blobs are fsynced before it.
753	
754	`serve --sync-mode=normal` trades that back for the older, narrower promise, the
755	process and not the machine, with power loss covered only as far as the last
756	checkpoint. It is worth about 1ms at p95 per message and nothing outside noise
757	across a whole suite, so take it only if you know why you want it. A server
758	started that way announces `sync normal` on its startup line, so a CI log
759	records the trade rather than hiding it.
760	
761	Ack latency itself is around 7ms at p50 and 9ms at p95 in either mode. It is set
762	by the blob fsyncs and by waiting for the single writer, not by this pragma, so
763	changing the mode is not the lever for making delivery faster.
764	
765	### Seeding an identity before it is handed over
766	
767	A leased address is an address, and quite often a test needs more than that: an
768	account that already exists, a user with a subscription, a teacher whose credits
769	have run out. `--seed-url` is the hook for that, and it exists today - it is not
770	planned work.
771	
772	```
773	authstunt serve --project demo --domain demo.test \
774	  --seed-url http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/test/seed
775	```
776	
777	The URL must be absolute, `http` or `https`, must carry no userinfo, and is
778	fixed at startup rather than taken per request, so a caller holding a run token
779	can never choose where this process sends a POST. A bad value fails at startup
780	instead of at the first lease. Redirects are refused for the same reason.
781	
782	Every acquire then POSTs to that endpoint before the lease is handed back, with
783	an `Idempotency-Key` header holding the lease id:
784	
785	```json
786	{
787	  "run_id": "…", "lease_id": "…", "identity_id": "…",
788	  "addr": "signup-8627b23ca1e5@demo.test", "role": "signup", "mode": "ephemeral"
789	}
790	```
791	
792	Your application creates whatever `role` means to it and answers:
793	
794	```json
795	{ "status": "seeded", "fingerprint": "user_8412" }
796	```
797	
798	`status` must be `seeded` or `skipped`. `fingerprint` is optional, free-form, and
799	recorded on the lease and in the audit ledger so a run can be traced back to the
800	row it touched; it is not returned to the caller. There is no shell on this path
801	by design: a seed hook that ran a command would turn a configuration file into
802	arbitrary code execution, and a postcondition is something an HTTP call states
803	just as well.
804	
805	That is what `seed_state` reports back on the lease:
806	
807	- **`skipped`** - no `--seed-url` is configured, or your endpoint answered
808	  `skipped`. This is what an out-of-the-box instance always returns.
809	- **`seeded`** - your endpoint ran and reported the account ready.
810	
811	A lease never comes back `pending`: the acquire has already settled by the time
812	it returns, so a caller never has to ask whether the account it was handed is
813	ready. Every failure is the same failure - a non-200, a timeout, a redirect, an
814	oversized body, a body that is not JSON, a status the schema does not name - and
815	all of them refuse the acquire with `lease_seed_failed` rather than handing back
816	an identity that is not known to be prepared. The endpoint's URL and response are
817	logged, not returned, because they belong to the application under test.
818	
819	`internal/personas` is the package all of this lives in: it turns a request for
820	an identity of some role into a lease, mints ephemeral addresses, walks the
821	pooled candidates, and calls the seed hook. It appears in `Layout` above and is
822	named here so the two match.
823	
824	One limitation, stated plainly: **nothing in this binary puts an identity into
825	the pool.** The pool is only ever read, so `mode: "pooled"` on a server with an
826	empty pool refuses every lease. Seeding prepares an identity that has already
827	been leased; it is not a way to populate a pool. Pooled mode is accepted but
828	unsupported, and this is part of why.
829	
830	### Mail for an address you did not allow
831	
832	A message addressed to any recipient outside the allowlist is accepted, stored,
833	and quarantined: kept as evidence and held back from the automated read path, so
834	a staging app that copies a real customer address cannot hand that person's mail
835	to a test.
836	
837	## Security
838	
839	Report a vulnerability to **security@authstunt.com** rather than in a public
840	issue. [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) says what is in scope and what is not, and
841	the "out of scope, by design" part is the half worth reading first: the host is
842	trusted, and the SMTP listener accepts every credential it is given.
843	
844	### Retention and deletion
845	
846	**Nothing is ever deleted.** Every message keeps its row, roughly two encrypted
847	blob files, and its ledger entries for as long as the data directory exists. The
848	periodic sweep expires runs and leases so their identities return to the pool; it
849	frees no disk. Size tracks how much mail an instance has ever accepted, not how
850	old it is.
851	
852	That is a storage note for a suite you point at one long-lived instance. It is a
853	more serious note if your mail carries personal data, and auth mail usually does:
854	
855	- The **raw message** is stored, not just the extracted code. Subject, bodies,
856	  `From`, `To` and `Cc` - whatever your template puts in a message about a real
857	  person is what lands on disk.
858	- **Quarantined mail is stored too.** Mail to an address outside the allowlist is
859	  held back from the automated read path, which is the point, but it is kept as
860	  evidence. A staging application that copies a real customer means that
861	  customer's mail is on your disk until you remove it.
862	- Bodies and extraction results are **encrypted at rest** with a key in the data
863	  directory. That protects the files if they are copied off the host. It is not
864	  deletion, and it is not a defense against anyone who can read the data
865	  directory, because the key is in it.
866	
867	**How to delete, today.** Delete the data directory. That is the whole mechanism,
868	and there is no finer-grained one: no retention window, no per-message delete, no
869	`authstunt purge`. So the deletion story is a layout decision you make up front
870	rather than an operation you run later:
871	
872	- Give each suite, or each CI job, its own `--data-dir` and remove it in
873	  teardown. An ephemeral container volume does this for you, and it is the
874	  reason the Quickstart uses one.
875	- Keep a shared long-lived instance only for a domain you own end to end, and put
876	  removing its data directory on a schedule somebody actually owns.
877	- If your organization has a data retention policy that applies to test systems,
878	  this instrument does not enforce it for you. Assume the directory is the unit
879	  of compliance.
880	
881	A finer-grained retention or purge surface is open backlog, not a planned
882	release.
883	
884	## Layout
885	
886	- `cmd/authstunt` - main binary
887	- `internal/*` - server internals: smtp, extract, api, store, secrets,
888	  personas, ledger, sse, relayconf, fsutil, mcp
889	- `packages/client` - `@authstunt/client`, the typed TypeScript client
890	- `packages/playwright` - `@authstunt/playwright`, the fixtures
891	- `examples/demo-app` - a signup flow with an emailed code, to test against
892	- `docs/transcripts` - recorded agent runs against the MCP surface
893	
894	Planned, not yet written: `web/` dashboard · `internal/flows`
895	
896	## Development
897	
898	Requires Go 1.26+. `go build ./...` builds, `go test -race ./...` tests,
899	`golangci-lint run` lints. The TypeScript packages each run `npm run verify`,
900	which type-checks, lints, builds, smoke-tests both module formats, and checks
901	the published shape with publint and arethetypeswrong before the tests.
902	
903	CI runs all of it, repeats the Go tests on Windows (where the key file is
904	protected by an ACL rather than mode bits), and adds a cross-platform build
905	matrix and a goreleaser config check.
906	
907	Development uses AI assistance under the quality bar documented in `CLAUDE.md`.
908	
909	## License
910	
911	MIT. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).
